caveats.t: Customs figures are values declared at the border by the reporting economy, not sales. Mirror rows disagree: the UK declares US$1.44bn of HS 97 exports to the US for 2025 while the US declares US$1.63bn of imports from the UK; Switzerland declares US$813m of exports to the US while the US records US$188m of imports from Switzerland; Hong Kong declares US$464m of exports to the UK while the UK records US$8.3m of imports from Hong Kong. Goods in transit, consignment moves, valuation rules and declaration points explain the gaps; the globe should show which side reported each arrow.

caveats.t: Trade is not the market: the Art Basel & UBS report puts US sales at 43% of the world by value in 2024 (UK 18%, China incl. Hong Kong 15%, France 7%), while US customs imports of art and antiques fell 15% to US$8.8bn and exports 7% to US$10.3bn in 2024 (USITC data), with France, the UK and Germany taking 56% of imports and 41% of exports and China 13% of exports. In 2025 US imports rose 13% to US$9.9bn and exports slipped 1%.
src: Art Basel & UBS Art Market Report 2025, pp.17–27
Art Basel & UBS Art Market Report 2026, ch.1

caveats.t: US tariffs: after the Supreme Court struck down the 2025 tariffs, the regime announced in July 2026 (10% or 12.5% on about 80 countries under Section 301) exempts works of art, antiques and collectors' items, following trade-body submissions including Cinoa's; separately, 50% tariffs announced on 20 July 2026 on Canadian imports do apply to contemporary and historical art, antiques, antiquities, stamps and coins. The 2025 tariffs had already pushed collectors towards bonded storage. Customs values are therefore mostly duty-free entries, and tariff shocks show up as timing shifts rather than as duty paid.

Freeports and bonded warehouses hold works in customs suspension: a shipment into the Geneva, Luxembourg or Singapore freeports, a UK bonded warehouse or Delaware Freeport is not an import for duty until it clears, so a move between two vaults can appear as an export from one economy with no matching import, or not at all. Geneva Freeport reported a 'significant increase' in clients over three years to mid-2025 as US tariffs and new EU import rules pushed collectors to hedge.

Switzerland is a transit and storage hub rather than a market of its size: it declared US$3.44bn of HS 97 exports in 2025 and US$2.41bn of HS 9701 exports (11.4% of the world), its largest declared corridor is to Germany (US$1.1bn, almost all paintings), and its exports to the US (US$813m) are more than four times what the US records arriving from Switzerland (US$188m). The Art Basel & UBS report records Swiss sales falling 3% in 2024; Swiss customs values should be read as movements, not Swiss buying.

caveats.t: Hong Kong's declared art trade is dominated by re-exports: it declared US$4.53bn of HS 9701 exports in 2025 (21.4% of the world, second only to the US) and US$1.93bn of HS 97 exports to the US alone, while receiving US$1.64bn from the US, US$601m from mainland China and US$327m from Japan. These are consignments moving through the auction and fair calendar, not Hong Kong production or consumption.

UK–EU change after 2020: from 1 January 2021 UK trade with EU members is declared at customs and enters HMRC statistics on a customs basis, so UK–EU art corridors before and after 2020 are not comparable; this is from memory and no page confirming it was opened.

The US exemption of art from the 2025 tariffs under the 'informational materials' exception (50 U.S.C. 1702(b)) is from memory; the Art Newspaper article opened (28 Jul 2026) describes the 2026 Section 301 exemption without naming the statute.
Hong Kong C&SD's distinction between domestic exports and re-exports of HS 97 was not read on a C&SD page; the re-export caveat rests on the corridor values themselves.
